What is drawn

Steve McCormick’s Figure 1, in three dimensions: one lump of radiation, the same initial data, evolved three ways by his code. On the left it is a perfect fluid at amplitude δm = 0.510; in the middle the same amplitude with the neutrinos (R_ν = 0.409 of the energy) streaming freely from ε₀ = 0.1; on the right the neutrinos again at δm = 0.535, above his threshold 0.528.

Each lump is 14 of his plasma shells, the Lagrangian shells his code follows (r from 0.12 to 3.2 in units of the lump’s size r_m), drawn at R/a, the areal radius with the background expansion divided out, so an undisturbed shell stands still. Colour is his compaction C = 2(M − M_b)/R at the shell; a shell turns white when it is falling in with 2M/R ≥ 1, the apparent horizon, where his code stops. The bead on each shell is that shell’s clock: it turns at the shell’s lapse A = ((1 − R_ν)ρ_b/e)^¼ against the background, so as the centre is squeezed its clocks slow down (to a tenth of the background rate at the fluid’s horizon). On the neutrino lumps the orange fans on every second shell are the neutrino intensity I(μ), divided by its mean, against the outward direction (μ = cos θ): a round flower is isotropic, a flower stretched out along the shell’s normal is light streaming out, one stretched inward is neutrinos falling in.

The charts are his own diagnostics of these runs: the peak of the compaction function, and the central densities of plasma and neutrinos, each against its background, as in his Figure 1. The dashed gold line at 2/3 is a reference only: it is the largest value of his amplitude δm = C_l − (3/8)C_l², reached at C_l = 4/3, the top of the range of the linear compaction for which his black holes form; it is not a threshold in this evolution.

His equations, as the page uses them

Metric ds² = −A²dt² + B²dr² + R²dΩ², r labelling the plasma shells. Γ ≡ D_rR and the Misner–Sharp mass M are tied by Γ² = 1 + U² − 2M/R, U = D_tR. Einstein: D_tM = −4πR²[(p + P_r)U + qΓ], D_rM = 4πR²(ρΓ + qU), D_tU = −M/R² − 4πR(p + P_r) + Γg, D_tΓ = 4πRq + gU, g = D_rA/A. Plasma: D_te = −(e + p)θ, (e + p)g = −D_rp + κq. Neutrinos: the transport equation for I(t, r, μ), with the moments e_ν = 2π∫I dμ, q = 2π∫μI dμ, P_r = 2π∫μ²I dμ, and collisions relaxing I toward isotropy at κ = H(T_b/T_dec)³(T/T_b)⁵; in these three runs κ = 0 after ε₀ (pure radiation, p = e/3, so A ∝ e^(−¼)). Compaction C = 2(M − M_b)/R, M_b = (4π/3)ρ_bR³. Apparent horizon: U + Γ = 0, a shell with 2M/R ≥ 1 and U < 0. Initial data: the growing mode of the gradient expansion for K(r) = A exp(−r²), δm = (2/3)K(r_m)r_m². Steve’s Γ is the radial gradient of the areal radius; it shares a letter with the peel step Γ = tanh(r/2) and nothing else.

Checked before this page ran (NU3D-CHECK-01)

The three runs are his: run with his own code (PBH_neutrino_simulation, commit eb7c4de of 11 Nov 2026) and his settings for Figure 1 (N = 400 shells, N_μ = 32, ε₀ = 0.1), his diagnostics reproduce the figure data archived in his repository row for row with no difference at all (231, 7926 and 3955 rows), and each run ends as his did: the fluid forms a horizon at ε = 4.035, the neutrinos at 0.535 at ε = 4.54, and at 0.510 they run to ε = 9 without one. The frames are recorded from the same runs, every Δε = 0.025.

Next to the moving matrix of balls (structural parallels, not identities)

A lump of his shells is layers of layers, each with its own clock, the lapse A: a flock of clocks inside one ball, slowing toward the centre as it is squeezed. The neutrino directions turn by aberration as the plasma accelerates and shears (his equation A4), the way light on the rim of the ball turns under a step. Whether the neutrinos move with the plasma or stream free is set by a ratio of two rates, the collision rate κ against the expansion rate H. The horizon is where a shell reaches 2M/R = 1. These are parallels of structure; the page draws his physics and nothing of the ball model.

Limits

Spherical symmetry, as in his paper. These are his pure-radiation runs with a fixed neutrino fraction and decoupling at ε₀ = 0.1, the case of his Figure 1, not the full thermal history. Shells are drawn at R/a and scaled by 0.55 for the view; fans are drawn on every second shell inside r = 2.1; the three lumps are placed side by side for comparison only. Only 14 of his 400 shells are drawn, and fans only on every second shell. His code stops at the first apparent horizon; the accretion after it is not followed here.
